title: One in Three Asian Americans With Serious Distress Goes Untreated, Largest NYC Study Finds
excerpt: A population-based study of 6,648 Asian American adults in New York City found that stigma, cost, and a lack of culturally matched therapists are leaving a fast-growing community without the mental health care it needs.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Over one-third of Asian Americans with serious distress in NYC go untreated.
  • Cultural stigma and cost are major barriers to mental health care access.
  • Asian Americans represent 17% of NYC's population but only 3.4% of licensed psychologists.
  • Community-based interventions may be more effective than traditional therapy models.
  • Mental health gaps contribute to physical health issues in Asian American communities.

Data from the 2023 Neighborhood Wellness Survey
New York City is home to one of the largest and fastest-growing Asian American populations in the United States. Yet a landmark study published in *Social Science & Medicine* has revealed that more than a third of Asian American adults experiencing serious psychological distress in the city are going without treatment — a gap driven by cultural stigma, prohibitive costs, and a stark shortage of therapists who look like or speak the language of their patients. The study, led by Dr. Thinh Toan Vu at the NYC Department of Health in collaboration with CUNY Graduate School of Public Health Professor Victoria Khanh Ngo, drew on data from the 2023 Neighborhood Wellness Survey — the largest population-based mental health survey of Asian American communities in New York City to date, with a representative sample of 6,648 adults across all five boroughs. ## The Numbers The findings paint a complex and troubling picture: Seven point four percent of Asian American adults reported experiencing serious psychological distress in the past 30 days. Among those in distress, 37.2 percent exhibited unmet mental health treatment needs, meaning they were not receiving counseling or medication despite needing it. While 64.2 percent of respondents with serious distress sought some form of help, many relied on informal sources — family, friends, community elders — rather than formal mental health services. In a culture where mental health has historically been treated as a private family matter rather than a medical one, this is not surprising. But it does mean that many are navigating anxiety, depression, and trauma without professional support. The barriers were consistent and deeply structural: 51 percent cited self-reliance as the reason they did not seek treatment. Forty-six percent pointed to cost. Forty-two percent said they simply did not know what services were available. > **""This gap underscores the need to expand culturally and linguistically responsive mental health services so that care better reflects the communities it is meant to serve," said Dr."** ## The Representation Gap Perhaps the most striking finding was the therapist shortage. Asian Americans account for 17 percent of New York City's population but only 3.4 percent of licensed psychologists in New York State. "This gap underscores the need to expand culturally and linguistically responsive mental health services so that care better reflects the communities it is meant to serve," said Dr. Vu. The study also identified structural factors tightly linked to poorer mental health: experiences of racial and ethnic discrimination, social isolation, and financial strain were all strongly associated with higher levels of psychological distress. Individuals who had experienced intimate partner violence were more likely to report both distress and help-seeking, suggesting that crisis can sometimes be the trigger that finally breaks through cultural reluctance. ## The Diaspora Dimension For the broader South Asian diaspora, the findings resonate beyond New York. The cultural barriers to mental health care identified in this study — stigma, self-reliance as a coping default, unfamiliarity with available services, and a shortage of culturally competent providers — are replicated in Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi, and Sri Lankan communities across the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

A separate 2026 paper published in the *International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health* by Jyoti Sinha at the University of Massachusetts Boston documented how South Asian immigrants face "multidimensional trauma stemming from immigration stress, sociocultural stigma, and systemic discrimination" — and how this chronic psychological burden directly contributes to the cardiovascular disease epidemic in South Asian communities. The connection between mental and physical health is increasingly impossible to ignore. Chronic stress, untreated anxiety, and social isolation do not just affect mood — they drive inflammation, metabolic dysfunction, and heart disease. For a population already facing elevated cardiovascular risk, the mental health gap is a physical health emergency. ## What Needs to Change The researchers point to several concrete steps: expanding culturally and linguistically responsive mental health services, integrating informal support networks — the family and community structures that Asian Americans already rely on — into formal care pathways, and investing in pipeline programs that increase the number of Asian American mental health professionals. Community-based interventions that meet people where they are — in temples, gurdwaras, community centers, and cultural organizations — may prove more effective than traditional clinical models for a population where walking into a therapist's office still carries stigma. "This is the largest study to date focusing on Asian American communities in NYC, a population that has been underrepresented in public health research despite being the fastest-growing demographic group in the city," said Dr. Vu. "By documenting these patterns, the study lays the groundwork for more targeted efforts."
Impact of Cultural Barriers
›Stigma prevents seeking professional help.
›Self-reliance is a common coping mechanism.
›Unfamiliarity with services limits access.
›Shortage of culturally competent providers.
For NRIs navigating the pressures of immigration, cultural dislocation, family expectations, and professional demands, the message is both clinical and personal: asking for help is not weakness. And the system needs to make asking easier. *The study was published in Social Science & Medicine (March 2026). Additional research from the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (February 2026).*
